interpretation: Normal: <42 mmol/mol (<6.0%). Pre-diabetes: 42-47 mmol/mol (6.0-6.4%). Diabetes diagnosis: ≥48 mmol/mol (≥6.5%). Poor control: >86 mmol/mol (>10.0%).
clinical_notes: Reflects average blood glucose over 2-3 months. Affected by haemoglobin variants, anaemia, and chronic kidney disease. Use fasting glucose if HbA1c unreliable.

interpretation: Normal: 62-106 µmol/L (male), 44-80 µmol/L (female). Elevated values suggest impaired renal function. Must be interpreted with eGFR.
clinical_notes: ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril) and ARBs may increase creatinine by 20-30% — this is expected and acceptable if rise is <30% from baseline. NSAIDs can also elevate creatinine by reducing renal blood flow. Monitor at baseline, 1-2 weeks after starting ACE/ARB, then annually.

interpretation: G1 (≥90): Normal. G2 (60-89): Mildly decreased. G3a (45-59): Mild-moderate decrease. G3b (30-44): Moderate-severe decrease. G4 (15-29): Severely decreased. G5 (<15): Kidney failure.
clinical_notes: Key for drug dose adjustments. Ramipril: reduce dose if eGFR <30. Metformin: avoid if eGFR <30, reduce dose if eGFR 30-45. Lithium clearance decreases with declining eGFR — monitor levels more frequently.

interpretation: Normal: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L. Hypokalaemia: <3.5. Hyperkalaemia: >5.5. Critical: >6.5 (cardiac arrest risk).
clinical_notes: ACE inhibitors and ARBs increase potassium — monitor at baseline and 1-2 weeks after initiation. Spironolactone combined with ACE/ARB significantly raises hyperkalaemia risk. Thiazide diuretics lower potassium. NSAIDs can also raise potassium via reduced renal excretion.

interpretation: Normal: 136-145 mmol/L. Hyponatraemia: <136 (mild 130-135, moderate 125-129, severe <125). Hypernatraemia: >145.
clinical_notes: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hyponatraemia, especially in elderly patients. SSRIs can also cause hyponatraemia via SIADH. ACE inhibitors rarely affect sodium. Monitor sodium within 2 weeks of starting thiazides in patients >65.

interpretation: Therapeutic: 0.4-0.8 mmol/L (maintenance), 0.8-1.0 mmol/L (acute mania). Toxic: >1.5 mmol/L. Potentially fatal: >2.0 mmol/L.
clinical_notes: ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce lithium clearance — monitor levels closely and consider 25-50% dose reduction when co-prescribing. NSAIDs also reduce lithium clearance. Dehydration, low-sodium diets, and thiazide diuretics all increase lithium toxicity risk. Take 12-hour post-dose trough levels.

interpretation: Normal: 7-40 U/L. Mild elevation (1-3x ULN): common with statins, usually benign. Moderate (3-10x): investigate. Severe (>10x): acute hepatitis, drug toxicity.
clinical_notes: Statins may elevate ALT mildly — routine monitoring no longer recommended unless symptoms. Discontinue statin if ALT >3x ULN with symptoms. Amlodipine rarely causes hepatotoxicity. Check baseline ALT before starting statins.

interpretation: Desirable: <5.0 mmol/L. Borderline high: 5.0-6.2. High: >6.2. Target for high-risk CVD patients: <4.0 or ≥40% reduction from baseline.
clinical_notes: Part of cardiovascular risk assessment. Treat with statins if QRISK3 ≥10% (primary prevention) or established CVD (secondary prevention). Non-HDL cholesterol is preferred over LDL for treatment targets.

interpretation: Normal: 3.9-5.5 mmol/L. Pre-diabetes (IFG): 5.6-6.9 mmol/L. Diabetes: ≥7.0 mmol/L (confirmed on two occasions). Hypoglycaemia: <3.9.
clinical_notes: Use when HbA1c is unreliable (haemoglobin variants, pregnancy). Thiazide diuretics and beta-blockers may impair glucose tolerance. Metformin is first-line if lifestyle measures insufficient.

interpretation: Normal: 0.4-4.0 mU/L. Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH 4-10 with normal T4. Overt hypothyroidism: TSH >10 or TSH elevated with low T4. Hyperthyroidism: TSH <0.1.
clinical_notes: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism — check TSH at baseline and every 6 months during lithium therapy. Amiodarone also affects thyroid function. Levothyroxine absorption reduced by calcium, iron, and PPI co-administration.

interpretation: Normal: <100 pg/mL (heart failure unlikely). Grey zone: 100-300 (possible HF). Elevated: >300 (heart failure likely). Very high: >1000 (severe HF or acute decompensation).
clinical_notes: Used to rule out heart failure in patients with dyspnoea. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line treatment for HFrEF and will lower BNP over time. Amlodipine is safe in heart failure (unlike other CCBs). Obesity can lower BNP — use higher thresholds.

interpretation: Normal (not anticoagulated): 0.8-1.2. Therapeutic on warfarin (most indications): 2.0-3.0. Mechanical heart valve: 2.5-3.5. Supratherapeutic (>5.0): high bleeding risk.
clinical_notes: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulants — avoid if possible, use paracetamol for analgesia. Amiodarone, fluconazole, and cranberry juice increase warfarin effect. Ramipril does not significantly interact with warfarin.
